list.listitem: Suspect leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) in patients with palpable purpura of the lower extremities. This is often self-limited and confined to the cutaneous superficial vascular plexus. Systemic involvement should be ruled out. C

A skin biopsy should be done for hematoxylin and eosin staining and direct immunofluorescence. Other things to consider: CBC with differential, chemistry, renal and liver function tests, urinalysis, pertinent infectious serologies (hepatitis, HIV, and/or anti-streptolysin O [ASO] titer), CXR, stool guaiac, ESR/CRP, antinuclear antibody, and other tests (ANCA, rheumatoid factor) if warranted. C
Provide supportive care if there is no systemic or organ involvement and no cutaneous ulceration or necrosis. C
Corticosteroids are the most widely used medication for severe cutaneous skin lesions (ulceration or bullae) and/or systemic disease. C
Rule out life-threatening diseases that require early treatment, such as disease associated with ANCA. C
LCV usually follows a benign course if there is no systemic involvement; monitor patient for 6 months or longer in those with abnormal UA or serum creatinine. C

background.definition: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) is a clinical and histological diagnosis characterized by neutrophilic inflammation affecting small vessels within the dermis (i.e., arterioles, capillaries, venules) , particularly post-capillary venules. The inflammation often leads to vessel wall damage. It encompasses a subset of diseases that express variably clinically and also overlaps with other vasculitic disorders.

list.listitem: LCV occurs in all ages and more commonly in females.
90% of cases occur in adults. The mean age is 47 years-old for adults and 7 years-old for children.
Incidence is 15 to 29 per million per year.
Incidence of cutaneous LCV is 15-38 cases per million/year
Idiopathic: 39.0%
Infection (meningococcemia and sepsis): 22.5%
Drug: 20%
Connective tissue disease: 11.7%
Neoplastic: 4.3%
Part of larger vessel vasculitis
Chronic or other systemic diseases
Allergies
Radiocontrast media
Mixed cryoglobulinemia
Rheumatoid vasculitis: 2% of all patients with RA
Levamisole-associated vasculitis
Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis
LCV may be related to vascular deposition of immune complexes formed in the setting of antigen excess with complement and neutrophil activation.
The inflammatory infiltrate often includes neutrophils, fibrinoid necrosis , and disintegrated nuclei.
LCV involving superficial and deep vessels is more likely to be associated with systemic disease.
Mechanisms may include idiopathic, infection, drugs, cryoglobulinemia, connective tissue disease, or neoplasm.
Suspect LCV in patients with palpable purpura of the lower extremities. The disease is usually limited to the skin, and although rare, systemic involvement should be ruled out. C

A skin biopsy will determine the involved vessel size and type of inflammatory infiltrate, which will aid in diagnosis. A punch biopsy should be done on an early lesion that is less than 24 hours old. The tissue can be bisected and sent for hematoxylin and eosin staining and direct immunofluorescence (except in children). C
Serologies can help determine the presence of systemic involvement. C
Rule out life-threatening diseases that require early treatment (e.g., ANCA-associated diseases). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Palpable nonblanching purpura on lower extremities without systemic signs or organ involvement
Younger patients with palpable purpura, arthralgias/arthritis, colicky abdominal pain and IgA+
Children <2 years old with palpable purpura in face and lower extremities, usually asymptomatic
Wheals last >24 hours, lesions burn more than itch, and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation occurs
Palpable purpura in cooler and dependent regions, arthralgias, and nephritis; associated with Hep C, low complement (espcially C4)
Positive autoantibodies to neutrophilic cytoplasmic antigens (ANCA); necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without asthma
Asthma, eosinophilia, and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation
Like Wegner's but without granulomas; cutaneous LCV, glomerulonephritis, alveolitis
Positive blood cultures, fever, and leukocytosis
Thrombocytopenia, anemia, fever, CNS, and renal complications

list.listitem: American College of Rheumatology criteria for cutaneous LCV: age >16 years old, medications that may have precipitated event, palpable purpura, cutaneous eruption, and positive biopsy. Having 3 or more items is 71% sensitive and 84% specific.
Chapel Hill Consensus Conference for cutaneous LCV: isolated cutaneous vasculitis without systemic involvement or glomerulonephritis.

Suspect cutaneous LCV in patients with palpable purpura in the lower extremities and possible symptoms of itching, burning, or stinging. Lower extremity edema and joint pain may also be seen. The purpura may last months before resolving.

Other cutaneous manifestations may include petechiae, infiltrative erythema, vesicles, nodules, ulceration, bullae, digital gangrene, and/or livedo reticularis. Some of these manifestations may indicate a more serious systemic vasculitis or vasculopathy. Urticarial vasculitis lesions differ from LCV in that they resemble urticarial wheals but typically last more than 24 hours and then resolve with postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.
Cutaneous lesions can be exacerbated by exercise, extreme temperatures, and prolonged standing.

Ask about recent medication changes, recent infections (upper respiratory, strep pharyngitis, hepatitis B and C, and HIV), vaccinations, and changes in diet. Also ask about any coexisting diseases such as collagen tissue disorders (RA, SLE, Sjogren's), Bechet's, inflammatory bowel disease, and systemic necrotizing vasculitides (Wegener's, Churg-Strauss, microscopic polyangiitis). Do a thorough review of systems to include: constitutional (fever, fatigue), head/neck (dry eyes and mouth, sinusitis, uveitis, mucosal ulcers, and lymphadenopathy), CV (chest pain, CHF, edema), pulmonary(wheezing/cough, hemoptysis), GI (abdominal pain, hematochezia), renal (hematuria, edema), musculoskeletal (myalgia, arthralgia) and neurological (mononeuritis).

Although cutaneous LCV is usually limited to the skin, constitutional symptoms can occur and may include fever, migratory small and large joint arthralgias, myalgias, and weight loss. Systemic involvement is rare but may include the renal, musculoskeletal (joints), and GI systems more commonly than the pulmonary and central nervous system.

Suspect systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis in patients with fever, necrotizing subcutaneous nodules, livedo racemosa, sinusitis, hemorrhagic nasal secretions, diffuse involvement of other organs (glomerulonephritis, pulmonary hemorrhage, granulomas in the lung), allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma, eosinophilia, inflammatory infiltrates in the wall of the vessels, and perivascular granulomas, and in patients not responsive to colchicine or dapsone.
No standardized workup exists. However, the main focus of testing is to exclude systemic involvement.

Skin punch biopsy should be obtained from a lesion less than 48 hours old. Two samples are submitted. One sample is placed in formalin for hematoxylin and eosin while the other sample is placed in Michel's medium for DIF (direct immunofluorescence). The sample should be bisected vertically and one half placed in formalin (H/E routing histologic staining) and the other half placed in Michel's medium (for DIF). The DIF can differentiate perivascular IgA versus IgG/IgM. IgA vasculitis is more often associated with systemic involvement (Henoch-Schoenlein purpura) and a potentially worse prognosis. The clinician should evaluate for systemic involvement (renal, connective tissue, infection and, in adults, malignancy).
Wedge biopsy should be considered when the involvement of medium vessels is suspected.

Serologies: A CBC with differential may aid in excluding other potential causes of the physical findings such as neutrophilia associated with sepsis/infection, eosinophilia in Churg-Strauss, thrombocytopenia in TTP or DIC, and abnormal counts that may indicate a myeloproliferative disorder.
Order serum creatinine, liver function tests, ESR or CRP, and urinalysis (for infection or hematuria).
Imaging: Order CXR to rule out pulmonary hemorrhage, asthma, chronic obstructive lung disease, pneumonia, autoimmune diseases, and malignancies.
Stool guaiac for possible GI complications especially in HSP.

If the clinical evaluation suggests urticarial vasculitis, systemic vasculitis, or underlying malignancy, consider ordering pertinent labs: ASO titers and HBV, HCV, and HIV serologies; throat cultures, fungal or bacterial cultures; complement levels (CH50, C3, C4); ANCA antibodies such as p-perinuclear ANCA/myeloperoxidase (MPO) and c-cytoplasmic ANCA/proteinase-3 (PR-3); antinuclear antibodies, dsDNA, Ro-SS/A, La-SS/B, and rheumatoid factor; and serum protein electrophoresis, cryoglobulins, visceral angiography, renal biopsy, and/or bone marrow biopsy.

In children, LCV is frequently HSP. This is a clinical diagnosis and for humane reasons, a cutaneous biopsy is not generally done. A history and physical, CBC, chemistry, UA, and stool guaiac are needed.
Suspect LCV in patients with palpable purpura on the distal lower extremities. There may be associated edema and joint pain. Confirm diagnosis with biopsy.

Although rare, it is important to look for systemic organ involvement and the extent of involvement. Exclude bacteremia, sepsis, infection, signs of connective tissue disease, underlying systemic disorders, malignancies, and systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis.

ANCA-associated vasculitis includes Wegner's granulomatosis, Churg-Strauss, and microscopic polyangiitis, which often have systemic organ involvement. They are detected in a patient's serum by indirect immunofluorescence or ELISA. The main 2 types of antibodies are perinuclear (p-ANCA) and cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) patterns. If a patient has a negative ANCA but is clinically suspicious, a renal biopsy should be considered.

If urticarial vasculitis is suggested, obtain serum complements. Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis is often associated with systemic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and SLE-related disorders.
If DIF (by skin biopsy) is positive for perivascular IgA, check renal function/hematuria and for potential malignancies.
If the patient is asymptomatic and without evidence of systemic involvement, provide supportive care. Avoid triggers and treat underlying causes (i.e., discontinue drugs, treat infections). C
Corticosteroids are the most widely used medication for severe cutaneous skin lesions and/or systemic disease, but are not recommended for long-term use. C
Consider colchicine or dapsone ± pentoxifylline for chronic or recurrent LCV. C
More potent immunosuppressants may be required for chronic recalcitrant LCV; consider corticosteroids and/or cytotoxic agent for systemic or ANCA-associated vasculitis. C
No large randomized control studies have been done.

Most patients with LCV will not require aggressive treatment, since most are self-limited and follow a favorable course. Supportive care includes pain control, rest, leg elevation, discontinuation of offending drugs, treatment of underlying diseases or infections, compression stockings, NSAIDs, and antihistamines. None have been shown to change disease course or prevent recurrence in clinical trials.

Systemic corticosteroids may be indicated for severe LCV, including ulcers or impending necrosis. The dose recommended is 0.5-1 mg/kg/day. Although no randomized prospective studies exist, efficacy has been suggested in case reports and reviews. Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended for long-term therapy.
Alternatives for skin limted LCV include colchicine, dapsone, or hydroxychloroquine.

Reports of patients with systemic manifestations suggest the beneficial use of early systemic corticosteroids in HSP to alleviate arthritis and abdominal pain. Some studies suggest oral steroid use may change the course of renal disease but not prevent recurrence. However, an RCT found that steroids in uncomplicated HSP did not decrease the risk of renal or acute GI complications.

For chronic or relapsing course, colchicine is recommended as first-line therapy, dapsone as second-line, and pentoxifylline +/- dapsone for third-line. Colchicine has been reported to be effective in multiple case reports for LCV as well as urticarial vasculitis. While a prospective RCT of 41 patients showed colchicine had no significant therapeutic effect, relapse occurred on cessation of treatment; therefore colchicine may be effective.

A few case reports have suggested effectiveness of steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, and methotrexate), IV immunoglobulins, or plasmapheresis for recalcitrant chronic LCV.
With systemic and possible ANCA-associated disease, systemic corticosteroids and/or a cytotoxic agent should be considered.
In a case series, diet control appeared to decrease recurrence; if food triggers are suspected, an allergy RAST test should be done prior to altering diet.
Avoid identified triggers to prevent recurrences.
Other remedies such as fish oil and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors for HSP have not shown to be effective.
Generally cutaneous LCV has a benign course without systemic or organ disease. C
However, if there is systemic involvement or signs of ANCA-associated vasculitis, prompt diagnosis is required because there is increased potential for mortality. C
Follow-up is required for at least first 6 months for all children and those with abnormal UA or serum creatinine. C
Natural history is unpredictable.
Most patients (60%) have an acute self-limiting cutaneous vasculitis lasting on average 3.7 months. Relapsing disease course occurs in approximately 20% and chronic disease in about 20%.
If there is systemic involvement or signs of ANCA-associated vasculitis, prompt diagnosis is required because there is increased potential for mortality.
Paresthesias, fever, absence of painful lesions, myalgias, arthralgias, cutaneous necrosis, and very elevated ESR are risk factors for systemic disease.
Cryoglobulins, arthralgias, and normal temperature are risk factors for chronic disease.
Severe abdominal symptoms, persistent purpura, and decreased F XIII are associated with higher risk factor in children for developing renal complications.
Adults having HSP with purpura above the waist, fever, high titers of inflammatory markers, prior infection, and age older than 50 years had a higher risk of renal involvement.
Studies show that there is potential for ESRD in up to 3% to 14% of children that have had LCV-induced glomerulonephritis.
Mortality reported as high as 1.9% in patients with systemic manifestations.
In a systematic review of 12 studies with 1133 children diagnosed with HSP, there was no long-term renal impairment if they had a normal urinalysis (UA).

Follow the UA for 6 months, but follow-up beyond 6 months is not required if the UA remains normal. Children with abnormal UA will require long-term follow-up. For adults, the follow-up period is not clearly defined, but strongly consider follow-up assessment of UA if on initial presentation the patient had an abnormal UA.
Perform at least a yearly clinical and serologic reevaluation in patients with relapsing or chronic disease.
